params.question: The video explains that post-polio residual paralysis is treated with tendon transfer, while cerebral palsy is treated with tendon lengthening. Which underlying mechanism explains this difference in surgical approach?

answers.text: PPRP produces rigid contractures from denervated muscles, while CP produces flail, lax joints from overactive muscles

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reverses the actual pattern. PPRP produces flail, hypermobile joints because the muscle has lost its nerve supply entirely. CP produces rigid contractures because spastic muscles are overactive and too tight.

answers.text: In PPRP, the paralysed muscle has lost its nerve supply entirely, so a functioning muscle must be redirected to replace it; in CP, muscles are overactive and spastic, so they need to be surgically released

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Anterior horn cell destruction in PPRP leaves the muscle without any nerve supply, necessitating redirection (transfer) of a working muscle. In CP, the muscle retains its nerve supply but is released from cortical inhibition, producing spasticity that is managed by lengthening the overactive muscle–tendon unit.

answers.text: Both conditions involve weakened muscles, but tendon transfer is chosen for younger patients and tendon lengthening for older patients

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The choice between transfer and lengthening is determined by the underlying pathology (LMN vs UMN), not the patient's age. A denervated muscle needs replacement by transfer; a spastic muscle needs release by lengthening.

answers.text: Tendon transfer is preferred in PPRP because sensation is absent, reducing post-operative pain; lengthening is preferred in CP because sensation is preserved

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sensation is completely normal in PPRP — poliovirus attacks only motor neurones. The treatment choice is driven by whether the muscle is paralysed (needing replacement) or spastic (needing release), not by sensory status.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the contrast table: PPRP destroys the anterior horn cell (no muscle innervation → flail joint → transfer a working muscle), while CP damages the brain (muscle still innervated but spastic → contracture → lengthen the tight muscle).
Well done. This LMN-vs-UMN distinction is the single most important concept in neuromuscular orthopaedics and drives every subsequent treatment decision.

params.question: Since cerebral palsy is caused by a non-progressive brain lesion, the orthopaedic deformities also remain stable throughout childhood.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. The narration explicitly states that while the brain lesion is static, 'the orthopaedic and functional consequences are dynamic, and they tend to worsen as the child grows.' Without proactive treatment, deformities often become considerably worse despite the non-progressive nature of the underlying brain injury.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Although the brain lesion in CP is static and non-progressive, the musculoskeletal consequences are dynamic. As the child grows, spastic muscles fail to elongate at the same rate as bone, leading to progressive contractures and worsening deformities that require proactive management.

interactions.label: A twelve-year-old boy with post-polio residual paralysis has a fixed equinovarus

params.question: A twelve-year-old boy with post-polio residual paralysis has a fixed equinovarus deformity and paralysed ankle dorsiflexors. The tibialis posterior muscle grades 4. A tendon transfer of tibialis posterior to the dorsum of the foot is planned to restore dorsiflexion. What must be done before the transfer?

answers.text: Begin six months of intensive strengthening exercises to improve the tibialis posterior to grade 5 before transfer

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A grade 4 muscle already meets the minimum donor requirement. The critical issue here is the fixed deformity — it must be corrected before any reconstructive procedure, regardless of donor muscle strength.

answers.text: Perform the transfer immediately to prevent the equinovarus deformity from worsening further

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Operating on an uncorrected fixed deformity violates the management hierarchy. The transferred tendon will be placed under abnormal tension, the joint cannot move through the range the tendon needs, and the patient ends up no better than before surgery.

answers.text: Correct the fixed equinovarus deformity first, so the transferred tendon can function across a mobile, plantigrade joint

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The management hierarchy requires corrective procedures before reconstructive ones. A tendon transfer onto a stiff, deformed joint is stretched under abnormal tension and cannot produce useful movement. Correcting the deformity first gives the transferred tendon the best chance of restoring functional dorsiflexion.

answers.text: Prescribe an ankle-foot orthosis for one year and defer the transfer, since conservative management alone may resolve the fixed deformity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An orthosis can prevent worsening or support a paralysed limb, but it cannot correct an established fixed bony deformity. Surgical correction of the equinovarus is needed before the reconstructive tendon transfer can proceed.

overallFeedback.feedback: Revisit the management hierarchy: conservative measures come first, then corrective procedures to address fixed deformity, and only then reconstructive procedures like tendon transfer. Skipping the corrective step dooms the transfer to failure.
Exactly right. The strict hierarchy — conservative, then corrective, then reconstructive — exists because reconstruction on an uncorrected deformity guarantees a poor result.

interactions.label: A five-year-old child with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy (GMFCS level II) has

params.question: A five-year-old child with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy (GMFCS level II) has dynamic equinus that limits walking, but no fixed contracture. Six months of physiotherapy and ankle-foot orthosis use have produced limited improvement. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Surgical Achilles tendon lengthening to permanently correct the equinus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tendon lengthening is reserved for fixed contractures or cases where less invasive measures have been exhausted. In dynamic equinus without a contracture, a reversible intervention should be tried before committing to surgery.

answers.text: Selective dorsal rhizotomy to permanently reduce lower-limb spasticity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Selective dorsal rhizotomy is an irreversible surgical procedure at the far end of the spasticity management spectrum. It is reserved for carefully selected children and is not the next step after conservative measures in focal dynamic equinus.

answers.text: Botulinum toxin injection into the gastrocnemius–soleus complex, followed by intensive physiotherapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Botulinum toxin temporarily blocks nerve signals to the overactive calf muscles, reducing spasticity for three to six months. This provides a window during which physiotherapy can consolidate gains in range of motion and strength — the appropriate next step on the spasticity management spectrum.

answers.text: Intrathecal baclofen pump implantation to control generalised spasticity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Intrathecal baclofen is indicated for severe, generalised spasticity, usually at higher GMFCS levels. It is not appropriate for focal dynamic equinus in a community-ambulant child at GMFCS level II.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the spasticity management spectrum: physiotherapy and orthotics → botulinum toxin (temporary, focal) → oral or intrathecal baclofen (generalised) → selective dorsal rhizotomy (permanent). Each step targets a different severity and distribution of spasticity.
Well done. Botulinum toxin sits at the right point on the spectrum — reversible, targeted, and paired with physiotherapy to consolidate the benefit.

params.question: A child with post-polio residual paralysis has paralysed ankle dorsiflexors but intact plantarflexors. Applying the principle that deformity results from 'the unopposed pull of whichever muscle still works,' which deformity develops, and what happens if a tendon transfer is performed without correcting any fixed component?

answers.text: Calcaneal deformity develops; the transfer will be too tight and restrict plantarflexion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Calcaneal deformity results from paralysed plantarflexors with intact dorsiflexors — the opposite muscle imbalance. With paralysed dorsiflexors and intact plantarflexors, the unopposed downward pull produces equinus, not a calcaneal foot.

answers.text: Equinus deformity develops; the transfer will succeed regardless because the donor muscle is strong enough

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: You correctly identified equinus, but donor muscle strength alone does not guarantee success. If the equinus has become a fixed contracture, the management hierarchy demands correction first — a transfer onto a rigid joint is stretched under abnormal tension and produces a poor result.

answers.text: Equinus deformity develops; if it becomes fixed, the transfer will fail because the tendon is stretched under abnormal tension across a rigid joint

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The intact plantarflexors pull the foot downward unopposed, producing equinus. If this becomes a fixed contracture, the management hierarchy demands surgical correction before tendon transfer — otherwise the transferred tendon works against a rigid joint and the outcome is poor.

answers.text: Varus deformity develops; the transfer must be delayed until the child stops growing to prevent recurrence

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Varus involves inward turning of the foot, driven by a different muscle imbalance such as unopposed tibialis posterior. Paralysed dorsiflexors with intact plantarflexors produce equinus — the foot points downward, not inward.

overallFeedback.feedback: This question combines two key principles: (1) identify which deformity results from the specific muscle imbalance (unopposed plantarflexors → equinus), and (2) recall that the management hierarchy forbids tendon transfer onto an uncorrected fixed deformity.
Excellent analysis. You correctly linked the 'unopposed pull' principle to the specific deformity and recognised why the management hierarchy must be respected before reconstruction.
